title: Conservation easement

definition.text: A conservation easement is a voluntary legal agreement in which a landowner gives a land trust or government the power to restrict uses of the land to protect its conservation value.

facts.text: It 'runs with the land', binding present and future owners, and is usually permanent.
Its key feature is reaching conservation goals while the land stays in private ownership and use; it does not make the land public.
Unlike land-use regulation, the owner places it on the property voluntarily.
Terms usually forbid or sharply limit subdivision and development, so the easement lowers the land's market value; one estimate puts the reduction at 35%-65%.
The holder must monitor the land and enforce the terms if they are broken.
By 2018 the US National Conservation Easement Database held over 130,000 easements covering 24.7 million acres.
In 2017 a ProPublica investigation criticised easements as a tax avoidance scheme costing billions in lost revenue.

contested_note: Critics say easement tax deductions are abused as a tax avoidance scheme, and US courts have penalised overstated easement values.

definition.text: In the United States, donating a qualifying conservation easement can earn the landowner federal income tax deductions and other tax breaks.

facts.text: The donation's value is the drop in the property's market value caused by the easement, set by a qualified appraiser.
To qualify the easement must be perpetual, held by a qualified public or nonprofit body, and serve a real conservation purpose.
Easements can also cut estate taxes, since heirs pay on farmland value rather than development value.
Some states give tax credits, and Colorado and Virginia let landowners sell them to others.

definition.text: Governments, nonprofits and donors often buy conservation easements outright, paying landowners directly.

facts.text: The US Farm Bill is a key funder; in 2014 it created the Agricultural Conservation Easement Program for farmland and wetlands.
States commonly fund conservation through real estate transfer taxes, bonds and lottery proceeds.
Many states and counties run programmes to buy agricultural easements that keep farmland from development.

definition.text: A debt-for-nature swap forgives part of a developing country's foreign debt in exchange for that country investing locally in conservation.

facts.text: Thomas Lovejoy of WWF proposed the idea in 1987, after the Latin American debt crisis cut indebted countries' ability to fund conservation.
The first swap, in 1987, let Conservation International buy US$650,000 of Bolivian debt for US$100,000 in return for conservation commitments.
Swaps work where default risk is high, so funders can buy debt well below face value; the government then pays in local currency for conservation.
Most swaps occur in tropical, species-rich countries with rapid deforestation and fairly stable political systems.
Since 1987 they have generated over US$1 billion for conservation in developing countries.
Swaps fell from about five a year in the late 1980s and early 1990s to about two a year after 2000, partly because commercial debt became pricier.
Swap experience shaped later tools such as conservation trust funds.

definition.text: Debt-for-nature swaps come in three kinds: commercial three-party swaps run by NGOs, bilateral swaps between two governments, and multilateral swaps among several.

facts.text: In a three-party swap an NGO buys debt from commercial banks on the secondary market and passes it to the debtor in return for conservation commitments.
In a bilateral swap a creditor country forgives part of another government's debt in exchange for environmental commitments.
Recorded three-party swaps raised nearly US$140 million and bilateral and multilateral swaps nearly US$900 million for conservation from 1987-2010.

title: Criticism of debt-for-nature swaps

definition.text: Critics argue that debt-for-nature swaps bring little real debt relief, send money to the wrong places and can harm local people.

facts.text: Debt relieved by swaps is under 1% of total external debt even in countries that use them often.
Early on, nearly three-quarters of swap funds went to Costa Rica, while Brazil, despite rapid deforestation, took little part.
Early swaps often overlooked people living on the land set aside, and some were labelled eco-colonialism.
Supporters, by contrast, describe swaps as deals in which every party benefits.

contested_note: Supporters call swaps a win for all parties, while critics say they give little debt relief, misdirect funds and can harm local people.
